nodes.label: Sarajevo/Zagreb syllable-switching slang mechanism
nodes.rationale: A footnote to the Appendix 8 short-story glossary (p.354/PDF 375) documents a genuine, historically attested word-game slang mechanism: switching a word's syllables, mechanically comparable to English pig-Latin-style play. Two documented lineages: (1) Sarajevo colloquial speech, productive and still current — attested examples: vozdra <- zdravo ("hi"), žemka <- kažem ("[I] say"), đido <- dođi ("come!"), žibje <- bježi ("run!/get away!"); (2) an older Zagreb layer, most widespread in the 1960s, now largely relic but with a handful of terms still in occasional use — attested examples: lima <- mali ("small/kid"), cobra <- braco ("bro"), Šomi <- Mišo (nickname), Njofra <- Franjo (nickname, kept alive longer because a Croatian cartoon dub used it as a catchphrase form of address). The footnote explicitly contrasts this with Belgrade's own extensive slang system, which the source states does NOT use syllable-switching as a mechanism — i.e. syllable-switching is geographically/dialectally bounded (Bosnian/Croatian urban colloquial, not pan-BCS), a productive morphological word-formation strategy (predictable input->output syllable transposition) rather than a closed list of slang lexemes. This is flagged by the dispatching instructions as the single most important content finding in the whole Serbian/Croatian/Bosnian corpus and is the most directly useful documented real-world mechanism for a conlang slang-synthesis system: it is a concrete, rule-based, generative slang-formation process (not just isolated lexical items) with attested input/output pairs across two distinct regional lineages.

nodes.label: Montenegrin as a fourth, distinct ijekavian national-standard variant
nodes.rationale: The book does not give Montenegrin its own [B]/[C]/[S] bracket letter and instead tells students to follow [J]/[S] forms, yet documents three concrete markers that make it a genuinely distinct system: systematic ijekavian character extending into negated-biti forms (nijèsam) and archaic-elsewhere adjectival endings (starijem); tj/dj -> ć/đ consonant realization (tjerati->ćerati, djevojka->đevojka, gdje->đe); and characteristic vocabulary (sjutra, zbòriti). The book also notes Montenegrin vocabulary leans closer to Serbian than to Bosnian/Croatian, while epic-song content itself (as sung by a Montenegrin performer) is pan-BCS cultural heritage independent of the dialect it's sung in — a genuinely useful content-vs-dialect distinction for synthesis work.

nodes.label: B/C/S Dialect-Tag Convention ([B]/[C]/[S])
nodes.rationale: Letters after a word signal either (a) the word is pan-BCS but a restricted-area alternate exists, or (b) two competing words exist and different standards prefer different ones. The source itself later clarifies (Ch. 26 of the Grammar volume) that this is a simplification of a frequency gradient, not a hard categorical split.
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Ekavian/Ijekavian Jat Reflex ([E]/[J])
nodes.rationale: Wherever Common Slavic jat historically stood, standard Croatian/Bosnian reflect it as ije (long) or je (short) — ijekavian — while standard Serbian mostly reflects it as e — ekavian; Serbian itself splits geographically (ekavian in most of Serbia proper, ijekavian in Bosnia, southwestern Serbia, Montenegro), so this axis cuts across the B/C/S national-standard split rather than mapping one-to-one onto it.
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Fleeting Vowels (Nepostojano A)
nodes.rationale: A stem-internal -a- that appears in a word's citation/nominative form but disappears in every other inflected form (e.g. adjective pametan -> pametno, pametna; noun pas -> Acc. psa; otac -> oca). Its loss can also trigger a consonant shift (nizak -> nisko, niska). Recurs across nouns, adjectives, and plural formation throughout the textbook.
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Genitive Case: Formation and Core Uses
nodes.rationale: Introduced in Lesson 4 as one of the most important BCS cases: masc./neut. Gsg mirrors the animate accusative; feminine takes -e (a-stem) or -i (consonant-stem). Governs prepositions like iz, kod, od, bez, and the invariant existential-negation word nema; also expresses partitive meaning ('some of') versus the accusative's whole-unit meaning.
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog
nodes.norm_label: genitive case: formation and core uses

nodes.label: Long vs. Short Adjective Forms
nodes.rationale: Most adjectives have both a short form (used after biti 'to be') and a long form (used elsewhere); some adjectives exist only in one form. A further 'longer' variant (extra -a- on the long masc./neut. genitive -og) is more common in Croatian and required when the adjective stands alone for a noun. The book explicitly warns against mapping this distinction onto English 'a/an' vs. 'the'.
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Montenegrin Excluded as a Fourth Standard Tag
nodes.rationale: Alexander & Elias-Bursać explicitly decline to add an [M] tag: despite Montenegro's 2006 independence and 2007 constitution naming 'Montenegrin' the official language, the 2008 codification process was too recent/unvalidated to treat as a fourth standard on par with B/C/S; Montenegro is described as sharing its associated cultural/religious history with Serbia, unlike the B/C/S split.

nodes.norm_label: montenegrin excluded as a fourth standard tag

nodes.label: Added Syllable (-ov-/-ev-) in Masculine Plural
nodes.rationale: Many masculine monosyllabic nouns insert -ov- (or -ev- after a soft consonant) before all plural case endings (drug -> drugovi, broj -> bròjevi, òtac -> òčevi); others (pas -> psi, dan -> dani) do not and must be memorized individually.

nodes.label: Regional/Colloquial Family Terms for Parents
nodes.rationale: Every region has its own colloquial word for 'father' and sometimes 'mother' (Bosnia: bàbo/nàna; Dalmatia: ćaća/papo; Zagreb's Zagorje: japa; Belgrade: ćàle/kèva), plus a pan-regional teen register (stara/stari/starci for parents). The source itself explicitly flags kèva as slang. Highest-value dialectal/register content in Lesson 9 for slang-synthesis purposes — first source-attested Belgrade slang term and first source-attested teen-register vocabulary set in the project.
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Second-Position Clitic Rule
nodes.rationale: The reflexive particle se and the short forms of biti ('to be': sam, si, je...) are unaccented clitics that cannot begin a sentence/clause; they must occupy the clause's second position regardless of where the main verb falls. This governs word order for a large class of everyday BCS verbs (zvati se, kaže se, etc.).
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Syllable-Switching Slang Formation Mechanism
nodes.rationale: Documented (per the project's extraction checklist) in `established/025_appendices7-8_literary_readings.md`, a footnoted slang-formation process producing forms like vozdra < zdravo and žemka < kažem via syllable reversal/switching, with regional (Sarajevo/Zagreb) and historical (1960s Zagreb) attestation — flagged as the single most important finding of the first-language test run and the obvious first candidate for Phase 3 mechanics analysis. Not itself contained in this chunk's 15 files but referenced by the project's own index as this language's flagship slang mechanism.

nodes.label: u-words vs. na-words (Locative Preposition Class)
nodes.rationale: Certain location nouns idiomatically pair with the preposition u ('in') and others with na ('on/at') for 'location,' a lexically-fixed pairing (e.g. škola, grad = u-words) that also surfaces B/C/S lexical-choice splits within the same semantic slot (bioskop [S] vs. kino [B,C] 'cinema'; kazalište [C] vs. pozorište [B,S] 'theater').
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Verbal Aspect: Perfective vs. Imperfective
nodes.rationale: Most BCS verbal ideas have two corresponding verbs sharing a root but differing in aspect: perfective (P) denotes a single completed action, imperfective (I) denotes repeated/in-progress/general action (e.g. kupiti P vs. kupovati I, both 'to buy'). A pervasive structural feature the textbook tracks explicitly from Lesson 2 onward.
nodes.community_name: Source Book Catalog

nodes.label: Yes/No Question Formation: da li vs. post-verbal li
nodes.rationale: Two syntactically distinct but semantically identical yes/no question strategies split along B/C/S lines: Serbian's most frequent pattern fronts da li before the verb, while Bosnian and Croatian's most frequent pattern places the clitic li directly after the verb. Independently confirmed across two different source books/lessons (Alexander & Elias-Bursać Lesson 1 and Magner Lesson 1).
